parts.title: Part I: Foundational Legal Research Topics
Part II: Advanced Legal Research Topics

embeds.title: Hierarchy of Authorities
embeds.blurb: A map of the legal authority hierarchy: what makes one source control another, the line between primary and secondary, and why the same case can bind in one courtroom and only persuade in another.

embeds.title: Applying the Hierarchy
embeds.blurb: Drills and applied exercises to test your command of legal authority: sort primary from secondary, tell binding from persuasive, decide when a statute controls, rank a full stack of authorities by binding effect, and place a court in its system.

embeds.title: Database Interface Explorer
embeds.blurb: Click through a generic legal database — header tools, the search bar, jurisdiction and content filters, the browse tabs, then a results page — and learn what every part does, so you can find the same features on any platform.

remove_paragraphs.reason: caption for Figure 2.1; the Database Interface Explorer replaces the static screenshot

chapters.title: The Question Method of Legal Research

embeds.title: Type the Question
embeds.blurb: Name the type of fourteen research questions — definitional, exploratory, focusing, or application — then pick the source family each one points to. The feedback explains the tell in every question's wording.

embeds.title: Notice of Claim — Research Sandbox
embeds.blurb: Work a real Arizona notice-of-claim problem through the question → answer → better-question cycle, logging every move in a research log.

replace_sections.title: Reverse Engineering the Question: A Demonstration
replace_sections.reason: the Reverse-Engineering the Question interactive walks the same Oakland Police v. Mayer Brown paragraph sentence by sentence

embed.title: Reverse-Engineering the Question
embed.blurb: Take a finished legal paragraph apart into the four research questions that built it, then watch those same questions become a synthesis table and an annotated outline — one color tying each question to its place in every form.

replace_sections.lead_md: Legal arguments are built by answering questions. Take a real paragraph from a federal opinion and turn each sentence back into the research question it answers.

embeds.title: The Types of Secondary Sources
embeds.blurb: Explore the nine major secondary sources, then re-sort them by the question they answer, their coverage, and their persuasive weight — and place each on a depth-and-breadth chart.
embeds.after: Types of Secondary Sources in Legal Research

embeds.title: Secondary Sources Practice
embeds.blurb: Run one question through the full cycle — match, mine, follow, leave — then practice the trust-and-timing judgment calls, including when an adopted Restatement may earn a cite.

embeds.title: Case Law Practice
embeds.blurb: Build a defensible case set, tell holding from dictum, and decide whether a flagged case is still good law.

embeds.title: Statutes Practice
embeds.blurb: Find an answer in a section's table of contents, read what a statute's status means for your research, and match a finding aid to what you know.

embeds.title: Regulations Practice
embeds.blurb: Navigate the CFR, choose between the CFR and the Federal Register, read shall/must/may/should, and check whether a regulation is still good law.

embeds.title: Across Sources Practice
embeds.blurb: Two problems — FMLA and Arizona workers' comp — each solved by pulling a statute, a regulation, and a case, with reveal-for-answer authority.

chapters.title: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research

embeds.title: Knowing When to Stop
embeds.blurb: Run the closing-out protocol, tell 'no results' from 'no law,' diagnose a stuck search, and draft an exportable research-closure note.

embeds.title: Diagnose the Broken Search
embeds.blurb: Zero results is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Practice telling ‘no results’ from ‘no law,’ finding what went wrong, and documenting closure.

chapters.title: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research

embeds.title: Catch the Fabricated Citation
embeds.blurb: A short brief, eight citations, one closed database. Retrieve each authority — or discover it does not exist — then classify it: supports, does not support, negatively treated, or fabricated. Feedback names the verification step that catches each failure.

embeds.title: Read the Docket
embeds.blurb: A fictional federal docket, entry by entry — including the two genuinely unintuitive features: newest-first ordering and the multi-part entry where one motion hides five documents.

embeds.title: Trace the Bill
embeds.blurb: The legislative process as a pipeline you can walk, with a deep-dive page for each history source — what it is, the weight it carries, the questions it answers — plus the anatomy of a committee report and the route-and-cautions checks. A short multi-page module; start on the overview.
embeds.after: The Most Important Sources and Their Weight

embeds.title: Weigh the Agency Materials
embeds.blurb: Seven client situations turning on which agency material controls: regulation versus FAQ, the binding-or-guidance test, and the answer that starts with naming the document type.

embeds.title: Pick the Parameters
embeds.blurb: Seven practice scenarios — set the right question type, first source, or closure call for each. The Pins Place client returns for deal work.

embeds.title: How the Machine Guesses
embeds.blurb: Feel prediction-without-retrieval: build a sentence one likely token at a time, watch the same mechanism assemble a perfect-looking fictional citation, walk the four-step framework, and sort what these tools can and cannot do.
embeds.after: How Generative AI Works and What That Means for Research

embeds.title: Verify the AI’s Work
embeds.blurb: A fluent AI answer with six citations — two solid, one disapproved, one real but cited for its opposite, two that do not exist. Run the four-step framework against the same closed database from Chapter 10, then decide how much of the answer survives.

chapters.title: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research

embeds.title: The Closed Universe
embeds.blurb: A fictional statute and three fictional cases — six exam-style questions answerable only from the provided sources, including the one the universe cannot answer. Format modeled on released exam materials; all content original.

appendices.title: How to Read a Secondary Source

embeds.title: How to Read a Secondary Source
embeds.blurb: A full encyclopedia entry on Arizona premises liability, read two ways: as a map of the doctrine, and for one question at a time — finding the sentence that answers you, taking its footnote, and reverse-engineering the headings into a research plan.

embeds.title: How to Read a Case
embeds.blurb: A real Arizona Supreme Court opinion, Markowitz v. Arizona Parks Board, read for class and then for one research question at a time — with a citator flag you must test against the question you are holding.

embeds.title: How to Read a Statute
embeds.blurb: Arizona's occupational-disease statute, read for one question at a time: navigate the chapter's table of contents, follow the cross-reference to the definition that controls, and recognize the subsections written for a different reader.

embeds.title: How to Read a Regulation
embeds.blurb: A DOJ rule on removing barriers in existing facilities, read from the authority note down — definitions, the operative verb, the Part's structure — and the question the codified text cannot answer.

downloads.title: Quick Tips & Research Checklists
downloads.desc: Two pages: the whole method in one breath, the four question types with where to look, and three checklists (before you search, every research cycle, closing out).
downloads.use: Keep it beside you for every assignment. Tick the boxes in the margins of your Research Log.

downloads.title: Research Log Template (spreadsheet)
downloads.desc: A blank log, one row per research cycle. Columns: Research Question, Method, Answer, Source, Next Question, Notes. The book's full scaffold also records Question Type and How This Answers My Question; add those two columns if you or your instructor want the whole eight-field entry.
downloads.use: Open it before your first exercise, write your macro question above the table, and add a row for every cycle you run.

downloads.title: Worked Example: Research Map, Research Log, and Annotated Outline
downloads.desc: One Arizona notice-of-claim problem run through all three tools, so you can see how a question moves from the map to the log to the outline.
downloads.use: Read it first, then try the Notice of Claim sandbox in Chapter 3 and build your own.

downloads.title: Key Takeaways and Common Pitfalls, by Chapter
downloads.desc: Every chapter's Key Takeaways and Common Pitfalls on one set of pages. Rebuilt automatically from the chapter text whenever the site is built.
downloads.use: Review before an exam or a project kickoff; check that you can restate each chapter in your own words.

downloads.title: Scholarship Research Checklist
downloads.desc: The ten-step method from Chapter 17 for seminar papers, notes, and comments.
downloads.use: Run it when the paper is assigned, and again before submission.
